<div id="block-receptionfaqsblockradio">
  
      <h2>Radio FAQs</h2>
    
      <div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Why can I hear a foreign radio station?
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<p><span>This normally happens in the summer months, due to high pressure weather conditions in the atmosphere, allowing radio signals to travel further. The cause is an atmospheric effect known as Sporadic-E and can last from a few seconds up to an hour or more.</span></p><p> </p>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Why is medium wave reception worse at night?
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<p><span ><span ><span >At night medium wave radio signals can travel much further than during the day. This means your radio is able to receive more radio channels either using the same frequency as the service you are listening to or adjacent to that frequency. The result is a higher level of interference and a deterioration in both the sound and coverage. </span></span></span></p>



</div></div><hr>

  </div>
<div id="block-receptionsimplecheckradio">
  
      <h2>Radio Help Guides</h2>
    
      <div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Troubleshooting FM radio
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<hr><blockquote><h3><span><strong>Basic Installation</strong></span></h3><p><span>It is important to check your installation is working properly and that your radio is in the best possible position. We have a </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/what-is-a-good-fm-radio-installation"><span><strong>basic installation guide</strong></span></a><span> to help you with this.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Works and warnings</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US" xml:lang="EN-US">Check whether there are any known </span><a href="/reception/works-warnings"><span lang="EN-US" xml:lang="EN-US"><strong>works or warnings</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US" xml:lang="EN-US"> that may be causing the problem.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter faults</strong> <strong>and frequencies</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">Use our </span><a href="/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter Checker</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> to check the transmitter is not undergoing any work and to see which FM radio services you can receive from your location.  </span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Hi-Fi radios</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">If you are using a Hi-Fi tuner and stereo reception is hissy, but mono is fine, your aerial may not be powerful enough. You may need to consider a loft or external aerial to solve your reception problem.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Weather</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">FM radio signals can be affected by fine weather including high pressure and the only solution is to wait for the weather to change, you should <strong>not</strong> re-tune during this time. </span>Our information on how clear skies and fine weather can affect your radio reception may be useful, please see our <a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/effect-of-tropospheric-ducting-on-radio"><strong>Weather Guide.</strong></a></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Pirate Radio</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">In some urban areas Pirate Radio can be a problem. The regulator, Ofcom, deals with Pirate Radio and you can report it using the </span><a href="https://www.ofcom.org.uk/make-a-complaint/complain-about-wireless-interference/illegal-broadcasting-pirates"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Pirate Radio form on the Ofcom website.</strong></span></a></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Distorted S and Z sounds (sibilance)</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This can happen when your radio receives more than one signal. The second signal is picked up by the radio moments after the first. For example you receive one signal directly from the transmitter and another is being reflected off a nearby hill. Try moving the radio or tuning to a different frequency.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Twittering and whistling</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This often sounds like birds tweeting and happens if there is another frequency being transmitted near the one you are listening to. This can commonly be caused by high pressure when, during fine weather, radio signals can travel much further than normal. These signals can be both UK and foreign stations. There is nothing that can be done and the problem will go away when the weather changes.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Hissing and fading</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This normally means that the signal you are receiving is not strong enough. See our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/hissing-and-fading-on-your-fm-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Hissing and Fading</strong></span></a><a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/hissing-and-fading-on-your-fm-radio"><span lang="EN-US">.</span></a></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Buzzing, clicking and pops</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This may mean an electrical item in your home or nearby, is interfering with the reception of your FM radio and is causing the buzzing, clicking or pops you can hear. See our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/buzzing-and-clicking-on-your-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Buzzing and Clicking</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"><strong>.  </strong>If you are still having problems see our sister site </span><a href="https://www.radioandtvhelp.co.uk/"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Radio and Television Investigation Service (RTIS)</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"><strong> </strong>for further information.</span></p><h3 class="MsoNormal"><strong>Distortion - fuzzy, gritty, scratchy sound<o:p></o:p></strong></h3><p class="MsoNormal">This is commonly caused by the FM signals being bounced off objects or hillsides and reaching your radio by different paths.<span style="mso-spacerun:yes;">  </span>Its technical name is multipath distortion. It is often worst in hilly or heavily built-up areas.<span style="mso-spacerun:yes;">  </span>Indoor portables are especially susceptible.<o:p></o:p></p><p class="MsoNormal">Distorted sound can also occur if your radio is off-tune.<span style="mso-spacerun:yes;">  </span>This can increasingly happen if your batteries are beginning to fail. Ensure your radio is correctly tuned-in, and check that your batteries are in good condition, or use mains power.  </p><h3><strong>Humming</strong></h3><p>If you are hearing a hum it is often linked to an issue with your mains adapter. You may need to check that all parts of your receiving system are fully earthed.</p><p class="MsoNormal"><o:p></o:p></p></blockquote><p> </p><blockquote><h2><strong><u>What to do</u></strong></h2><p>If your radio is a portable, try moving the aerial to different angles. You could also try a different position in the room. Window sills and high shelves are good places for radios; avoid putting them close to radiators or electronic equipment such as computers, mobile/cordless phones or TV sets.</p></blockquote><blockquote><p><span lang="EN-US">The telescopic aerial fitted to stereo portables is a compromise and the radio will often only give really good results if connected to an external aerial. If that’s not possible, switch to mono as it will usually sound better. Some sets do this automatically. </span></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Make sure you are tuned to the best frequency for your area, as you can often pick up more than one signal. Use our </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults/#/undefined"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter Checker</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> to find the best frequencies for your location.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Qualified Installer</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">The BBC cannot recommend individual installers. The <strong>CAI (</strong></span><a href="https://www.getmeviewing.org.uk/"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Confederation of Aerial Industries</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US">) is a recognised trade body which can put you in touch with one of its members in your area.</span></p></blockquote>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Troubleshooting MW Radio
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<hr><blockquote><p> </p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Basic Installation</strong></span></em></p></blockquote><blockquote><p><span lang="EN-US">It is important to check your installation is working properly and that your radio is in the best possible location. We have a </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/what-is-a-good-medium-wave-long-wave-installation"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>basic installation guide</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> you can read.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Works and warnings</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Check whether there are any known </span><a href="/reception/works-warnings"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>works or warnings</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> that might be causing the problem.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter faults</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">By using our </span><a href="/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults/"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter Checker</strong>,</span></a><span lang="EN-US"> you can check what MW radio services are available at your location. It will also show you any transmitter faults. </span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Weather</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">AM reception can vary a great deal from day to night because of differences in the atmosphere. You may get good, clear reception during the day, but after sunset the signal may fade or become distorted. This is why you can often hear radio stations from outside the UK at night. </span>Our information on how clear skies and fine weather can affect your radio reception may be useful, please see our <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/effect-of-tropospheric-ducting-on-radio"><strong>Weather Guide</strong></a><a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/effect-of-tropospheric-ducting-on-radio"><strong>.</strong></a></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Buzzing, clicking and pops</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">This may mean an electrical item in your home, or nearby, is interfering with your MW radio. This is causing the buzzing, clicking or pops sounds you can hear. See our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/buzzing-and-clicking-on-your-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Buzzing and Clicking</strong></span></a><a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/buzzing-and-clicking-on-your-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>.</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"><strong> </strong>If you are still having problems see our sister site </span><a href="https://www.radioandtvhelp.co.uk/"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>RTIS</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> for further information.</span></p></blockquote>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Radio reception problems due to high pressure
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<hr><blockquote><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Effect of Weather on Reception.</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Weather-related problems tend to happen mainly in the summer, when high pressure can cause a radio signal to travel further than it would normally. This is known as tropospheric ducting. For more information see our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/effect-of-tropospheric-ducting-on-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>tropospheric ducting</strong></span></a><a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/effect-of-tropospheric-ducting-on-radio"><span lang="EN-US">.</span></a></p><p><span lang="EN-US">If this distant radio signal is on the same frequency as the one you are listening to it can cause a reception problem. This is because your radio will struggle decoding two radio stations on the same frequency. This is known as co-channel interference</span></p><p><span lang="EN-US">The effect can last from a few hours to a few days and can cause intermittent effects on the service during that time.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>What  to do:</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">There is nothing that can be done but to wait until the weather changes. We have no control over it. </span></p><p><span lang="EN-US">If your problem is due to the weather, it should go away once the weather changes.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Works and warnings</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Check our </span><a href="/reception/works-warnings"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>works and warning page</strong> </span></a><span lang="EN-US">to see if there any current weather problems.</span></p></blockquote>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">What type of radio aerial do I need?
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<blockquote><hr><h3><em><strong>FM Radio</strong></em></h3><p>The most common FM radio aerial on a portable radio is a telescopic one.  To get the best reception extend the aerial fully and move the aerial and radio around until you get the best reception.  If using a hi-fi with a wire aerial, again extend as much as possible to get the best signal.</p><p>External aerials are also available for FM radio and will significantly improve reception. The aerial and cables need to be well maintained and you will need a radio that has an option to connect an external aerial.  </p></blockquote><blockquote><p><em><strong>AM Radio</strong></em></p><p>A radio which can tune to medium and long wave services usually has an aerial built in, which you cannot see. As the aerial is directional, by simply turning the radio you will be able to get the best reception. AM does not use the telescopic aerial.</p></blockquote><blockquote><p>Some hi-fi’s have external AM aerials that tend to look like many wires wound around a plastic loop. This needs to be rotated to find the best signal.</p></blockquote><blockquote><p><em><strong>DAB radio</strong></em></p><p>You need to have a suitable DAB aerial to receive DAB services. Portable DAB radios will usually have a telescopic one, but if you are retro-fitting a DAB radio into a car, you may need to add a DAB aerial. </p><p>External aerials are also available for DAB  and will significantly improve reception. The aerial and cables need to be well maintained and you need a radio with the option to connect an external aerial. Unlike the other services, all the predictions of DAB coverage are for indoor coverage.</p><p> </p><img src="/reception/sites/default/files/inline-images/radio%20aerials.jpg" data-align="center" data-entity-uuid="ba75bda6-c955-4349-9704-76dfcec37c5c" data-entity-type="file" alt="Examples of radio aerials" width="1920" height="1080" data-caption="DAB, FM and AM aerial examples"><p>                                                          </p><p> </p></blockquote>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">FM Radio in the car
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<blockquote><h2 paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{163}" paraid="938652277">Fading and Hissing </h2><p paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{196}" paraid="2015564692">If you normally can receive a service, but you are now finding it is fading in and out, or you can hear hissing, this could be down to one of three things. The first is a fault with the local FM transmitter. Secondly, if you know your location, you can use our <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults/#/undefined" rel="noreferrer noopener" target="_blank">transmitter checker </a>to see whether there is a problem. Thirdly, if not, then you will need to check the radio and aerial to confirm they are both working properly.  </p><h2 lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{524f35ce-2379-4d8e-9b60-4a65c52cda63}{43}" paraid="531753238" xml:lang="EN-GB">Interference </h2><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{524f35ce-2379-4d8e-9b60-4a65c52cda63}{51}" paraid="1658760408" xml:lang="EN-GB">Poor FM reception can also be caused by equipment used in the vehicle. For example, phone chargers or dash cams sometimes cause interference and affect your radio signal. Try unplugging the items to see if one of them is causing any interference. </p><h2 paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{213}" paraid="1716339103">Reception in Tunnels </h2><p paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{219}" paraid="788626479">Depending on the specific tunnel and station, Radio reception can cut out or be lost when driving through tunnels. If the tunnel is deep, the radio waves will not reach into the centre, so your radio cuts out. Some tunnels are fitted with signal distribution systems both for FM and DAB so the signal will not be lost while in the tunnel. Or it could be “To help maintain the radio signals within the tunnel” </p><h2 paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{229}" paraid="345098173">Tuning </h2><p paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{235}" paraid="1977410635">Most FM car radios have a Radio Data System (RDS) built in. We use the RDS to ‘tell’ your radio if there is a better or stronger frequency for the radio service you are listening to, as you travel around. However, if you are using a frequency, you have preset and there is no radio service on that frequency in your location, then the RDS may not work. At that point you will need to tune your radio until you find a signal. </p><h2 paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{249}" paraid="286070051">Aerials </h2><p paraeid="{a7ed067c-f804-496a-aec5-a23a875d77e1}{255}" paraid="213559333">If you are having continuous reception problems, check your car aerial for damage. If you have an extendable aerial, make sure it is fully extended to give the best possible reception. </p><h2 paraeid="{173ab1bd-4cae-4e8d-a51f-8a4c132c9f7a}{12}" paraid="1687804698">Local Radio Travel News </h2><p paraeid="{173ab1bd-4cae-4e8d-a51f-8a4c132c9f7a}{18}" paraid="1387925445">The RDS system is set up to detect local radio travel news. The way to turn traffic announcements on and off on varies between radios. Check your car manual for yours. </p><p><span lang="EN-US"><img src="/reception/sites/default/files/inline-images/car_1.jpg" data-entity-uuid="846a0a87-86aa-455f-aee9-65a7b0040a5b" data-entity-type="file" alt="car radio" width="1920" height="1080"></span></p></blockquote>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">AM radio in the car
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{e3f8f3d4-ce5e-451f-8d47-77720f35cce4}{248}" paraid="1494438835" xml:lang="EN-GB"><strong>Interference from car electrical systems </strong></p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{13}" paraid="382234101" xml:lang="EN-GB">Interference to MW reception in a car can be caused by many electrical systems within your car. From the ignition system to windscreen wipers or indicators. It usually sounds like whining or crackling sound, depending on the cause. Turning each element on and off to see if it goes away is one method to determine the cause but you may need to speak to an auto specialist  </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{26}" paraid="1372960763" xml:lang="EN-GB">  </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{36}" paraid="287887754" xml:lang="EN-GB"><strong>Interference from other electrical equipment</strong> </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{47}" paraid="901077109" xml:lang="EN-GB">Other causes of interference to MW radio in the car can include mobile phone chargers and dashcams. Check that connections are secure and cables are not damaged and see if the interference goes away of you move the equipment to other areas in the car.   </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{62}" paraid="1543442994" xml:lang="EN-GB">  </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{65}" paraid="1042031944" xml:lang="EN-GB"><strong>On the move </strong> </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{68}" paraid="1157881736" xml:lang="EN-GB">MW radio can also be affected by structures such as bridges and tunnels. </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{71}" paraid="324392126" xml:lang="EN-GB">In simplistic terms, the size of the MW wavelength is bigger than the radius of the entrance and struggles to reach into the tunnel or under the bridge. FM wavelengths are smaller so can usually reach in further by bouncing along the tunnel walls before they lose too much power  </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{74}" paraid="310488159" xml:lang="EN-GB">There’s nothing that can be done to improve this until you drive out from the tunnel or away from the bridge. </p><p lang="EN-GB" paraeid="{6b683f9e-2b59-40a0-8b0b-996a5190018a}{74}" paraid="310488159" xml:lang="EN-GB"> </p><p><img src="/reception/sites/default/files/inline-images/car_0.jpg" data-entity-uuid="f0e10de6-a265-4860-bcf0-30dfe18e30bc" data-entity-type="file" alt="car radio" width="819" height="461"></p>
</div></div><hr>

  </div>
<div id="block-receptiononlyguides">
  
      <h2>Radio Reception Help Guides</h2>
    
      <div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Buzzing and clicking on your Radio
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<hr><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Thermostat</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">The buzzing and clicking lasts from a few seconds to a minute at a time. Switch off heating systems and see whether the problem goes away. If the problem persists when you turn the heating system back on, the problem could be with the thermostat, which may need to be repaired or replaced.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Light switches</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">To find out if a particular switch is causing the problem, try turning the lights off one at a time.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>LED lights</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Many people are now using low power LED lights instead of the more traditional varieties. However, if the original light used a transformer rather than directly running off the mains, it is possible the transformer is causing the interference. This is because the transformer would have been designed to operate at the higher power and not the lower power the LED lights use. This has the potential to cause electrical interference.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Street lamps</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Street lamps can sometimes cause buzzing and crackling sounds on your FM radio. Keeping a note of when each lamp comes on and goes off will help to identify whether this is the cause of your interference. If it is, contact your local council.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Passing traffic</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">A faulty or uncompressed engine can cause a distinct buzzing 'whine' which varies with engine speed - motorcycles tend to be the worst. Try to move your radio away from the street or use an external aerial.</span></p><p><em><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Electric motor</strong></span></em></p><p><span lang="EN-US">An electric motor is used in many appliances such as electric lawnmowers, washing machines, drills and hairdryers etc.  A faulty motor can cause electrical interference. Check any appliance with an electric motor by moving your radio away from it to see whether the sound improves. If you have several appliances with electric motors you may need to turn them all off and try the above one at a time.</span></p><p> </p><p> </p><p><span lang="EN-US">With all of these potential causes, it is worth keeping a log for at least two weeks to determine whether there are any patterns or trends to the interference.</span></p>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Hissing and Fading on your FM radio
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<hr><blockquote><p><span lang="EN-US">This can be due to:</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Reduced transmitter power</strong></span></h3><p><span>Use our </span><a href="/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults"><span><strong>Transmitter Tool</strong></span></a><span> to see whether your local transmitter is currently affected by maintenance work.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Stereo Signal</strong></span></h3><p><span>Try moving the radio to another position, such as near a window, higher up, or another room. If you get hiss when listening to a stereo signal try switching to mono.  Stereo reception needs a stronger signal than mono.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Aerial</strong></span><span><strong> </strong></span></h3><p><span>If you have a portable radio you will be able to pick up more of the receivable signal if your telescopic aerial is fully extended. For hi-fi systems check your aerial isn’t broken or become loose. If you have an external or loft aerial check they are functioning correctly.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Tuning to the wrong transmitter</strong></span></h3><p><span>Use our </span><a href="/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults"><span><strong>Transmitter Tool</strong></span></a><span> to check you are tuned to the best frequency for your area, as you can often pick up more than one signal.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Weather</strong></span></h3><p><span>Very occasionally, the weather, usually high pressure, can result in a weakened signal. There is nothing anyone can do about this and the only answer is to wait for the weather to change. For more information see our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/radio-reception-problems-due-to-high-pressure"><span><strong>how weather can affect radio reception</strong></span></a><span>.</span></p></blockquote><p> </p>
</div></div><hr>
<div class="initHideChild hideChild hiddencontentblock">
  <span aria-expanded="false" aria-haspopup="true" class="bttn" onclick="this.parentNode.classList.remove('initHideChild');this.parentNode.classList.toggle('hideChild');">
    <h3 class="gel-great-primer title">Troubleshooting FM radio
    <i class="gelicon gelicon--down"></i></h3>
</span>
<div class="dropdown-menu gel-body-copy" id="works-warning-">
<hr><blockquote><h3><span><strong>Basic Installation</strong></span></h3><p><span>It is important to check your installation is working properly and that your radio is in the best possible position. We have a </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/what-is-a-good-fm-radio-installation"><span><strong>basic installation guide</strong></span></a><span> to help you with this.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Works and warnings</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US" xml:lang="EN-US">Check whether there are any known </span><a href="/reception/works-warnings"><span lang="EN-US" xml:lang="EN-US"><strong>works or warnings</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US" xml:lang="EN-US"> that may be causing the problem.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter faults</strong> <strong>and frequencies</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">Use our </span><a href="/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter Checker</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> to check the transmitter is not undergoing any work and to see which FM radio services you can receive from your location.  </span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Hi-Fi radios</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">If you are using a Hi-Fi tuner and stereo reception is hissy, but mono is fine, your aerial may not be powerful enough. You may need to consider a loft or external aerial to solve your reception problem.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Weather</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">FM radio signals can be affected by fine weather including high pressure and the only solution is to wait for the weather to change, you should <strong>not</strong> re-tune during this time. </span>Our information on how clear skies and fine weather can affect your radio reception may be useful, please see our <a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/effect-of-tropospheric-ducting-on-radio"><strong>Weather Guide.</strong></a></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Pirate Radio</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">In some urban areas Pirate Radio can be a problem. The regulator, Ofcom, deals with Pirate Radio and you can report it using the </span><a href="https://www.ofcom.org.uk/make-a-complaint/complain-about-wireless-interference/illegal-broadcasting-pirates"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Pirate Radio form on the Ofcom website.</strong></span></a></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Distorted S and Z sounds (sibilance)</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This can happen when your radio receives more than one signal. The second signal is picked up by the radio moments after the first. For example you receive one signal directly from the transmitter and another is being reflected off a nearby hill. Try moving the radio or tuning to a different frequency.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Twittering and whistling</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This often sounds like birds tweeting and happens if there is another frequency being transmitted near the one you are listening to. This can commonly be caused by high pressure when, during fine weather, radio signals can travel much further than normal. These signals can be both UK and foreign stations. There is nothing that can be done and the problem will go away when the weather changes.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Hissing and fading</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This normally means that the signal you are receiving is not strong enough. See our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/hissing-and-fading-on-your-fm-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Hissing and Fading</strong></span></a><a href="/reception/help-guides/fmmwlw-radio/hissing-and-fading-on-your-fm-radio"><span lang="EN-US">.</span></a></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Buzzing, clicking and pops</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">This may mean an electrical item in your home or nearby, is interfering with the reception of your FM radio and is causing the buzzing, clicking or pops you can hear. See our guide on </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/help-guides/fmmw-radio/buzzing-and-clicking-on-your-radio"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Buzzing and Clicking</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"><strong>.  </strong>If you are still having problems see our sister site </span><a href="https://www.radioandtvhelp.co.uk/"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Radio and Television Investigation Service (RTIS)</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"><strong> </strong>for further information.</span></p><h3 class="MsoNormal"><strong>Distortion - fuzzy, gritty, scratchy sound<o:p></o:p></strong></h3><p class="MsoNormal">This is commonly caused by the FM signals being bounced off objects or hillsides and reaching your radio by different paths.<span style="mso-spacerun:yes;">  </span>Its technical name is multipath distortion. It is often worst in hilly or heavily built-up areas.<span style="mso-spacerun:yes;">  </span>Indoor portables are especially susceptible.<o:p></o:p></p><p class="MsoNormal">Distorted sound can also occur if your radio is off-tune.<span style="mso-spacerun:yes;">  </span>This can increasingly happen if your batteries are beginning to fail. Ensure your radio is correctly tuned-in, and check that your batteries are in good condition, or use mains power.  </p><h3><strong>Humming</strong></h3><p>If you are hearing a hum it is often linked to an issue with your mains adapter. You may need to check that all parts of your receiving system are fully earthed.</p><p class="MsoNormal"><o:p></o:p></p></blockquote><p> </p><blockquote><h2><strong><u>What to do</u></strong></h2><p>If your radio is a portable, try moving the aerial to different angles. You could also try a different position in the room. Window sills and high shelves are good places for radios; avoid putting them close to radiators or electronic equipment such as computers, mobile/cordless phones or TV sets.</p></blockquote><blockquote><p><span lang="EN-US">The telescopic aerial fitted to stereo portables is a compromise and the radio will often only give really good results if connected to an external aerial. If that’s not possible, switch to mono as it will usually sound better. Some sets do this automatically. </span></p><p><span lang="EN-US">Make sure you are tuned to the best frequency for your area, as you can often pick up more than one signal. Use our </span><a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/reception/check-for-transmitter-faults/#/undefined"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Transmitter Checker</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US"> to find the best frequencies for your location.</span></p><h3><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Qualified Installer</strong></span></h3><p><span lang="EN-US">The BBC cannot recommend individual installers. The <strong>CAI (</strong></span><a href="https://www.getmeviewing.org.uk/"><span lang="EN-US"><strong>Confederation of Aerial Industries</strong></span></a><span lang="EN-US">) is a recognised trade body which can put you in touch with one of its members in your area.</span></p></blockquote>
</div></div><hr>

  </div>

DAB FAQs Why am I unable to receive Local Radio, or National Radio such as BBC Radio Scotland, on my DAB Radio? The BBC's local and national radio services are carried on local commercial DAB Multiplexes. Please see our help page to see how DAB multiplexes work , Therefore, you may not be receiving this service, as there is not a commercial DAB service in your local area. To check what coverage of DAB services are available in your locality, please see our  Transmitter checker tool . My DAB reception has started to drop out, is this due to poor reception? Firstly, poor reception might be down to poor coverage, so it is best to check you are in a DAB coverage area. Use our transmitter tool , which will tell you what national and local DAB services are available in your locality. Secondly, If you are in a good coverage area, and are still receiving poor DAB reception please try our Problem Assistant for further advice.   How can weather affect DAB reception? DAB reception is rarely disrupted by high-pressure weather conditions, but under some circumstances, signals from very distant transmitters can cause reception to break up, or be lost for periods of time. If you suspect this - particularly if you are also getting interference on FM - wait until the weather changes. Can LED Lights Interfere with my DAB Reception? There is a possibility some LED Lights can cause interference to DAB and FM Radio Reception, particularly if LED lights are used to replace halogen lights, and retain the original transformer.  This is because the power used is lower, and is forced to work outside of its normal operating parameters, resulting in electrical impulse interference. For more information on interference, please see our RTIS site DAB Help Guides What is a good DAB installation? Coverage and location Your radio must be in a good DAB coverage area to receive BBC services. Have a look at our  Transmitter Checker   to see what BBC services you can receive where you are.   If you live in a basement flat, or your building is steel-framed or reinforced concrete, coverage may be affected.   Tuning Most DAB radios can be tuned easily at the touch of a button. Sometimes a full scan is required. Portable radios should be tuned in a location in your home where the best possible signal is received. Most DAB radios come with built in signal strength meters which can be helpful.  From time to time radios should be re-tuned in order to discover new stations.    Telescopic aerials Telescopic aerials on portable radios should be fully extended to receive a good signal.  Tilting and swivelling the aerial will help to get the best signal.  Broken aerials may affect reception.     Outdoor aerials An externally mounted aerial can be attached to many types of DAB portable radio and hi-fi systems. DAB aerials are different from FM or TV aerials, so you need a good quality DAB-specific aerial.  An indoor aerial may be good enough, but for the best reception use an outdoor one. Even the best amplifier will still add some noise to the television signal it is amplifying/boosting that could result in picture break up. A good amplifier should have a filter built in that only allows the signal you want to be boosted and not any unwanted signals. Otherwise, all the unwanted signals will also be boosted, which can cause pictures to break up. Problems using amplifiers Amplifiers themselves are a common source of reception problems. For example, if water were to get into a masthead type, they can start to boost the result of the fault. This could be unwanted signals and result in picture loss on your own television and, maybe, those living nearby. To check, remove the power from the amplifier and see whether the problem goes away.   There are three types of amplifier – masthead, set-back and distribution. All these need a power supply to work. Masthead These fit directly under an outside aerial and usually the best type of amplifier to fix weak signals. Set-back These fit between the aerial socket in the wall and your television. Distribution These split the TV signal from a single aerial and allow the signal to be sent to several different televisions in the building.   Combined amplifiers Some amplifiers are a mix of the above. For example, some masthead amplifiers are also distribution amplifiers. Some can also combine television and FM radio signals.   Attenuators When to use an Attenuator If you are experiencing pixellation or picture break up, it may be that your signal is too strong as this often presents itself similarly to a weak signal. This is likely to happen if you live close to a transmitter. Attenuators can be used to decrease the incoming signal if it is too strong without distorting it. It is effectively the opposite of an amplifier, though the two work by different methods. While an amplifier provides gain, boosts the signal, an attenuator provides loss, reduces the signal. Attenuators are always a compromise and should only be used if absolutely necessary. They come in a variety of powers; in most cases a small reduction is all that is needed. Thirdly, if not, then you will need to check the radio and aerial to confirm they are both working properly.   Interference  Poor FM reception can also be caused by equipment used in the vehicle. For example, phone chargers or dash cams sometimes cause interference and affect your radio signal. Try unplugging the items to see if one of them is causing any interference.  Reception in Tunnels  Depending on the specific tunnel and station, Radio reception can cut out or be lost when driving through tunnels. If the tunnel is deep, the radio waves will not reach into the centre, so your radio cuts out. Some tunnels are fitted with signal distribution systems both for FM and DAB so the signal will not be lost while in the tunnel. Or it could be “To help maintain the radio signals within the tunnel”  Tuning  Most FM car radios have a Radio Data System (RDS) built in. We use the RDS to ‘tell’ your radio if there is a better or stronger frequency for the radio service you are listening to, as you travel around. However, if you are using a frequency, you have preset and there is no radio service on that frequency in your location, then the RDS may not work. At that point you will need to tune your radio until you find a signal.  Aerials  If you are having continuous reception problems, check your car aerial for damage. Switch off heating systems and see whether the problem goes away. If the problem persists when you turn the heating system back on, the problem could be with the thermostat, which may need to be repaired or replaced. Light switches To find out if a particular switch is causing the problem, try turning the lights off one at a time. LED lights Many people are now using low power LED lights instead of the more traditional varieties. However, if the original light used a transformer rather than directly running off the mains, it is possible the transformer is causing the interference. This is because the transformer would have been designed to operate at the higher power and not the lower power the LED lights use. This has the potential to cause electrical interference. Street lamps Street lamps can sometimes cause buzzing and crackling sounds on your FM radio. Keeping a note of when each lamp comes on and goes off will help to identify whether this is the cause of your interference. If it is, contact your local council. Works and warnings Check whether there are any known works or warnings that may be causing the problem. Transmitter faults and frequencies Use our Transmitter Checker  to check the transmitter is not undergoing any work and to see which FM radio services you can receive from your location.   Hi-Fi radios If you are using a Hi-Fi tuner and stereo reception is hissy, but mono is fine, your aerial may not be powerful enough. You may need to consider a loft or external aerial to solve your reception problem. Weather FM radio signals can be affected by fine weather including high pressure and the only solution is to wait for the weather to change, you should not re-tune during this time. Our information on how clear skies and fine weather can affect your radio reception may be useful, please see our Weather Guide. Pirate Radio In some urban areas Pirate Radio can be a problem. The regulator, Ofcom, deals with Pirate Radio and you can report it using the  Pirate Radio form on the Ofcom website. Distorted S and Z sounds (sibilance) This can happen when your radio receives more than one signal. The second signal is picked up by the radio moments after the first. For example you receive one signal directly from the transmitter and another is being reflected off a nearby hill. Try moving the radio or tuning to a different frequency. Twittering and whistling This often sounds like birds tweeting and happens if there is another frequency being transmitted near the one you are listening to. This can commonly be caused by high pressure when, during fine weather, radio signals can travel much further than normal. These signals can be both UK and foreign stations. There is nothing that can be done and the problem will go away when the weather changes. Hissing and fading This normally means that the signal you are receiving is not strong enough. See our guide on Hissing and Fading . Buzzing, clicking and pops This may mean an electrical item in your home or nearby, is interfering with the reception of your FM radio and is causing the buzzing, clicking or pops you can hear. See our guide on Buzzing and Clicking .  If you are still having problems see our sister site Radio and Television Investigation Service (RTIS)   for further information. Distortion - fuzzy, gritty, scratchy sound This is commonly caused by the FM signals being bounced off objects or hillsides and reaching your radio by different paths.   Its technical name is multipath distortion. It is often worst in hilly or heavily built-up areas.   Indoor portables are especially susceptible. Distorted sound can also occur if your radio is off-tune.   This can increasingly happen if your batteries are beginning to fail. Ensure your radio is correctly tuned-in, and check that your batteries are in good condition, or use mains power.   Humming If you are hearing a hum it is often linked to an issue with your mains adapter. You may need to check that all parts of your receiving system are fully earthed.   What to do If your radio is a portable, try moving the aerial to different angles. You could also try a different position in the room. Window sills and high shelves are good places for radios; avoid putting them close to radiators or electronic equipment such as computers, mobile/cordless phones or TV sets. The telescopic aerial fitted to stereo portables is a compromise and the radio will often only give really good results if connected to an external aerial. If that’s not possible, switch to mono as it will usually sound better. Some sets do this automatically.  Make sure you are tuned to the best frequency for your area, as you can often pick up more than one signal. Use our Transmitter Checker  to find the best frequencies for your location. Qualified Installer The BBC cannot recommend individual installers. The CAI ( Confederation of Aerial Industries ) is a recognised trade body which can put you in touch with one of its members in your area.

  <h3 id="thebbcistheworldsleadingpublicservicebroadcaster">The BBC is the world’s leading public service broadcaster</h3>
<p>We’re impartial and independent, and every day we create distinctive, world-class programmes and content which inform, educate and entertain millions of people in the UK and around the world.</p>
<p>We do this across:</p>
<ul>
<li>A portfolio of television services, including the UK’s most-watched channel BBC One and our multi award-winning channels for children, as well as national and regional television programmes and services across England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales</li>
<li>Ten UK-wide radio networks, providing the best live music broadcasting in the UK, as well as speech radio which informs, educates and entertains. We also have two national radio services each in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and local radio stations across England and the Channel Islands, providing an invaluable and unique service to listeners across the UK</li>
<li>Our digital services including BBC News, Sport, Weather CBBC and CBeebies, iPlayer and BBC Sounds, BBC Red Button and our vast archive</li>
<li><a href="/aboutthebbc/whatwedo/worldservice">BBC World Service</a> television, radio and online on more than 40 languages</li>
</ul>
<p>Established by a <a href="/aboutthebbc/governance/charter">Royal Charter</a>, the BBC is principally funded through the <a href="/aboutthebbc/governance/licencefee">licence fee</a> paid by UK households.     /* Scans the DOM to find annd return the page projectId
     * encoded in a url of a comment node */
    function lookupProjectId() {
            const walker = document.createTreeWalker(
                document.head,
                NodeFilter.SHOW_COMMENT,
                null,
                false
            );

            while (walker.nextNode()) {
                const comment = walker.currentNode.data;

                const urlMatch = comment.match(
                    /https:\/\/production\.bbc\.co\.uk\/isite2\/project\/[^"]+/
                ); 

                if (urlMatch) {
                    const url = new URL(urlMatch[0]);
                    const parts = url.pathname.split("/");
                    const projectIndex = parts.indexOf("project");
                    let projectId = parts[projectIndex + 1] ?? null;
                    return projectId;
                }
            }
    }

    function getCookie(name) {
        const nameEQ = name + "=";
        const cookiesArray = document.cookie.split(';');
        for (let i = 0; i < cookiesArray.length; i++) {
            let cookie = cookiesArray[i].trim();
            if (cookie.indexOf(nameEQ) === 0) return cookie.substring(nameEQ.length);
        }
        return null;
    }

    document.querySelectorAll('input[name="demoMode"]').forEach((radio) => {
        radio.addEventListener('change', function () {
            if (this.value === 'on') {
                const d = new Date();
                const days = 30
                d.setTime(d.getTime() + (days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000));
                const expires = "expires=" + d.toUTCString();
                document.cookie = `ckns_ipagesDemoMode=on; ${expires}; path=/`;
            } else {
                document.cookie = `ckns_ipagesDemoMode=; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 UTC; path=/;`;
            }
            window.location.reload(1)
        });
    });

    window.onload = function () {
        const demoModeCookie = getCookie('ckns_ipagesDemoMode');
        document.getElementById('demoModeOn').checked = demoModeCookie === 'on';
        document.getElementById('demoModeOff').checked = demoModeCookie !== 'on';
    };

    checkValidDevToolCookie()
</script>

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy0z.visible_text: Planned Powys rail centre not built despite £70m spend - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World Asia UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Planned Gibraltar-sized rail testing centre has cost taxpayers £70m but hasn't been built Image caption, The project is based at the former Nant Helen opencast coal mine in Powys By Daniel Davies Wales political correspondent Published 12 September 2026 Updated 9 hours ago The future of a proposed rail-testing centre that has received £70m of taxpayers' money but still has not been built is to be decided by the Welsh government. The Global Centre of Rail Excellence (GCRE) has not found the private-sector funding it needs as the risk is "too great" for potential investors, its boss has said. Launched five years ago, the project is based at the former Nant Helen opencast coal mine near Ystradgynlais, Powys. Ministers are now being asked to approve plans for a data centre there, which GCRE hopes will attract more funding for the rail project. The Welsh government said GCRE - which it owns - has been "exploring a range of projects to revitalise" the site. "We are working with the company to assess next steps, in light of our productivity mission," a spokesperson added. The Welsh government has given GCRE £50m since it was set up by Labour in 2021. The former Conservative UK government also provided £20m. GCRE hoped to find £330m from private backers to transform the mine near Bannau Brycheiniog national park - also known as the Brecon Beacons . Image source, GCRE Image caption, An artist's impression of the proposed GCRE Two 4.3 mile (7km) electrified tracks for testing trains would loop around a site roughly the size of Gibraltar. With other facilities, GCRE said it could create more than 1,000 jobs. It was supposed to be up and running in 2025, but has been delayed until 2030. The scheme was inherited by Plaid Cymru when it won the Senedd election in May. GCRE chief executive Simon Jones said there was demand in the rail industry for the services the company would provide "but we can't carry on using public money on this forever so a decision needs to be made". Jones added that there had been "detailed conversations" with an energy and data centre company, but said he could not name it due to commercial confidentiality. GCRE wants to complete those talks this year so a contract can be signed. "And we need to be in a position where we know whether the railway is going ahead or not at the moment we sign that contract," he told BBC Politics Wales . "If the government decides this is something that it wants to do, if we are able to execute the contract with the data centre partner, then five years from now we could be in a situation where we see trains running around this site." Image caption, GCRE's chief executive Simon Jones says there is demand in the rail industry for the services it could provide GCRE has spoken to potential investors around the world, but failed to secure funding. "I can list off a whole load of what would sound like excuses about macro-economic conditions, the long tail of Covid, etcetera, but essentially it comes down to risk appetite from the investment market," Jones said. "This is an unknown proposition that we have got here. There is risk around being able to create the UK's first purpose-built high speed rail testing facility, and that risk is too great for the market to take on its own in current circumstances." Welsh Conservative Member of the Senedd Andrew RT Davies, who visited the site as chairman of the last Senedd's economy committee, said: "The government needs to get its act together, make a quick decision. "Is it going to continue to back this site for regeneration purposes or is it going to re-purpose it for other reasons?"
